changelog.summary: Stories researched for 8 milestones.

meta.adoptionDefinition: Mainstream adoption: the year the technology reached widespread, routine use, roughly 10% or more of its potential market or standard practice in its sector.
meta.securityGuidanceNote: AI-generated research to prompt discussion, not security advice. References link to the official publishers; check the current version of each. Engage qualified cyber security experts, and your regulator where relevant, before acting.

milestones.title: Nuclear fission to grid power

research.what: Hahn and Strassmann observe fission in Berlin; Meitner and Frisch explain it.

change.what: Calder Hall connects to the UK grid.

milestones.note: War diverted the science into weapons first; civil power came through state programmes.

refs.label: https://www.euronuclear.org/glossary/calder-hall/

adoption.what: Nuclear supplies a significant share of electricity in leading economies.

gb.note: Nuclear provides firm low-carbon baseload on the GB grid. Ageing AGR closures and new capacity (Hinkley Point C, Sizewell C, SMRs) shape GB adequacy and inertia.

security.note: Digital instrumentation and control adds safety-critical cyber exposure.

milestones.title: HVDC transmission

research.what: Uno Lamm begins work on high-voltage mercury-arc valves at ASEA.

change.what: Gotland link enters commercial service in Sweden.

milestones.note: A long engineering road from valve research to a dependable link.

provenance.qaNote: All cited links are broken; downgraded until a new source is found.

refs.label: https://ieeemilestones.ethw.org/Milestone-Proposal:Gotland_HVDC_Link
Modern Power Systems: HVDC fifty years on

gb.note: HVDC carries GB's interconnectors and offshore wind links (e.g. Western Link, Eastern Green Link). It is central to moving Scottish and offshore wind south and easing constraints.

security.note: Adds digital control and communications to transmission and distribution assets.

milestones.title: Silicon solar cell

research.what: Bell Labs demonstrates the first practical silicon photovoltaic cell.

change.what: Vanguard 1 satellite flies on solar power.

milestones.note: Fast to first use because space could pay any price. Cheap terrestrial solar took another 50 years.

adoption.what: Solar becomes a mainstream source of new power capacity worldwide.

gb.note: GB has more than 18 GW of solar, mostly embedded on distribution networks. This drives the need for better visibility and forecasting.

security.note: Inverters and turbine controllers are networked and often vendor-managed remotely.

milestones.title: Utility-scale wind

research.what: NASA and the US energy research agency run the MOD-0 turbine programme.

change.what: First commercial wind farm opens in New Hampshire.

milestones.note: Oil shocks gave government research a sharp push into energy.

adoption.what: Wind becomes a mainstream share of new power capacity in Europe and the US.

gb.note: Wind is GB's largest renewable source, and offshore wind is central to Clean Power 2030. It drives constraint, balancing and network reinforcement needs.

security.note: Inverters and turbine controllers are networked and often vendor-managed remotely.

milestones.title: Lithium-ion battery

research.what: Goodenough’s Oxford group identifies the lithium cobalt oxide cathode.

change.what: Sony launches the first commercial lithium-ion cell.

milestones.note: The same chemistry family later made grid-scale storage viable.

adoption.what: Lithium-ion becomes the standard battery in laptops and mobile phones.

gb.note: Lithium-ion is the dominant chemistry in GB grid-scale BESS, which provides frequency response and balancing.

security.note: Battery management and dispatch systems are networked and remotely controllable.

milestones.title: High-temperature superconducting cable

research.what: Bednorz and Müller at IBM Zurich discover high-temperature superconductors.

change.what: A superconducting transmission cable is energised in a US utility grid.

milestones.note: Still niche: cooling, cost and reliability set the pace.

gb.note: Could add capacity in congested urban GB networks without new rights of way. I did not confirm any GB transmission deployment.

security.note: Adds digital control and communications to transmission and distribution assets.

milestones.title: Perovskite solar

research.what: Miyasaka’s group reports perovskite photovoltaic cells.

change.what: First commercial perovskite-on-silicon modules ship.

milestones.note: Durability, not efficiency, set the pace.

gb.note: Higher-efficiency modules would mean more embedded solar per site on GB distribution networks, adding to the challenge of forecasting distribution-connected generation. I found no evidence of GB deployments.

security.note: Inverters and turbine controllers are networked and often vendor-managed remotely.

refs.label: Panasonic: Miyasaka 2009 first perovskite solar cell
pv magazine: Oxford PV commercial perovskite tandem modules 2024

milestones.title: Fusion power

research.what: JET, a European publicly funded tokamak at Culham, produces first plasma.

change.what: Not yet landed. UK STEP targets a prototype plant around 2040.

milestones.note: The longest arc in the model and still rising.

refs.label: https://stepfusion.com/why-fusion/
https://stepfusion.com/why-fusion/

gb.note: STEP at West Burton aims to show fusion electricity around 2040. It has no near-term effect on GB network planning.

security.note: Digital instrumentation and control adds safety-critical cyber exposure.

milestones.title: Tandem solar at volume

research.what: Perovskite research from 2009, tandem cells from the mid-2010s.

change.what: Perovskite–silicon tandem modules move from niche shipments to volume manufacturing.

milestones.note: Depends on proving 25-year field durability.

basis.label: Industry roadmaps following first commercial shipments (2024)

gb.note: Higher-efficiency modules would raise output per rooftop and per hectare, adding to distributed solar on GB distribution networks. Oxford PV is a UK-origin company.

security.note: Inverters and turbine controllers are networked and often vendor-managed remotely.

refs.label: pv magazine: Oxford PV mass production 2027
Oxford PV roadmap

aiLevers.bottleneck: No proof yet that perovskite-silicon tandem modules last 25 years outdoors; accelerated tests designed for silicon don't capture perovskite-specific degradation, and outdoor data covers months.

levers.note: ML screening of capping layers, interface and passivation chemistries, and encapsulant choices for stability. Published work covers capping-layer selection; tandem-scale gains remain unproven.
Deep-learning analysis of luminescence images to track degradation, proposed for production-line quality control and yield. Currently lab-stage research on perovskite cells, not tandem factories.

refs.label: Solar Power World – Tandem PV demonstration manufacturing (Apr 2026)
refs.quote: is targeting high-volume manufacturing in 2028

refs.label: PatSnap – Technical barriers to long-term tandem stability
refs.quote: current perovskite-silicon tandem prototypes have demonstrated stability over periods measured in months, not decades

milestones.title: AI in grid control rooms

research.what: Machine-learning forecasting for wind, solar and demand.

change.what: AI-assisted forecasting and dispatch become routine control room tools, as NESO’s Volta programme (with Alphabet’s Tapestry on the Grand Optimiser) intends.

milestones.note: Assurance, explainability and cyber resilience will set the pace, not model capability.

basis.label: NESO: Volta programme

provenance.qaNote: The Volta programme and Grand Optimiser are confirmed. The Grand Optimiser sources describe design-stage deliverables (architecture plan, roadmap, interface mock-up), and NESO's innovation annex expects about 10 more Volta projects over five years. I found no source saying AI dispatch will be routine in 2027, so that year looks optimistic and the 2028–2030 range looks more likely. The 2017 researc

refs.label: https://www.neso.energy/news/volta-programme-powering-future-dispatch-tapestry-energy-moonshot-x-moonshot-factory-alphabets-innovation-lab-bring-ai-our-control-room

gb.note: NESO is building AI decision support on the Open Balancing Platform to cut balancing and constraint costs as renewable variability grows.

security.note: Brings software and data into control-room decisions, so data integrity and model security matter.

aiLevers.bottleneck: Moving validated ML forecasting and optimiser prototypes into live control room systems: real-time data integration, verification and validation, explainability and operator trust.

levers.note: ML demand and renewables forecasters, Faculty's Advanced Scheduling Adviser and Tapestry's Grand Optimiser give operators dispatch suggestions in one security-constrained optimisation, with humans still in control.
Co-simulating multiple digital models across operational timescales, plus cross-validation that simulates live retraining, to test optimiser and forecast behaviour before it touches real dispatch.
Structured verification and validation (Smith Institute), audit trails and explainable outputs build the assurance evidence that NESO operators need before they sign off on operational use.

refs.label: ENA Smarter Networks Portal – Volta: Real Time Prediction (NIA2_NESO105)
refs.quote: to meet the next TRL level, the prediction models need to be integrated into the real control room systems

refs.label: ENA Smarter Networks Portal – Volta: Grand Optimiser Design Philosophy (NIA2_NESO107)
refs.quote: it is necessary to conduct a validation and verification stage, where the design is tested in a modular approach

refs.label: NESO – AI First design discovery and prototyping

Process-control and quality analytics on newly started cell lines, aimed at yield, utilisation and the week-long formation/ageing step. Plausible, but no sodium-specific source found.
Degradation and lifetime models trained on early field data could support bankability. They could also help re-engineer battery management for sodium-ion voltage behaviour.

aiLevers.bottleneck: The strategy is still at evidence-gathering stage. The vision names six adoption barriers: data access, incentives, regulation, security, systems integration and skills.

levers.note: Core focus of the vision and review: AI for forecasting, planning, optimisation and coordination of flexibility and network operation. The review urges faster roll-out of already-proven AI applications.
Yu says AI surrogates can replicate complex physical simulations and run power-system studies orders of magnitude faster. This supports grid planning and scenario testing.
Automated algorithms, such as EV charging optimisation and automated demand response, and AI control-room assistance. The review also flags market-gaming risks and a need for governance of autonomy.
The vision asks how consenting and appraisal, which work to fixed decision points, cope with fast-changing AI modelling. No concrete AI approvals tool is described, and decisions stay human.

story.research: In 2022, research teams at NVIDIA (FourCastNet), Huawei (Pangu-Weather) and DeepMind (GraphCast) built machine-learning global weather models that rivalled ECMWF's physics-based high-resolution forecasts.

aiLevers.bottleneck: Per-route permits and a weak business case: only 11 sites ran by mid-2026 against a 50-site target, and some municipalities quit FY2026 trials.

levers.note: Digital twins of specific routes, such as the open-sourced V2XSim Kashiwa-no-ha scene, test roadside-sensor cooperation and rare edge cases before driverless operation, cutting on-road testing for each site.
Scenario-based simulation and logged driving data could build the safety case for each route faster for public-safety-commission permits and vehicle certification. Humans still decide.
Open-source AI driving stacks such as Autoware and ROS 2 planners let operators reuse perception and planning across sites instead of tuning a bespoke system for every route.
AI-assisted remote monitoring could let one supervisor oversee several vehicles, and demand data could guide route choice. This tackles staffing costs, which drive the weak business case.

research.what: Westinghouse engineer Roy J. Wensley built Televox, a machine that answered telephone calls and carried out switching actions in response to tones and simple sound commands, building on his earlier supervisory remote-control work. change.what: Televox units were used to report reservoir water levels and control water flow remotely over the telephone, and the humanoid-dressed version became a widely publicised 'mechanical man'.

milestones.title: Moving-coil cone loudspeaker (Rice–Kellogg)

research.what: General Electric engineers Chester Rice and Edward Kellogg worked out the direct-radiator principle: a small, light cone driven by a coil, set in a baffle, giving even response across the middle frequencies. They also designed a power amplifier to drive it. Origin: Rice & Kellogg, 'Notes on the Development of a New Type of Hornless Loudspeaker', Journal/Transactions of the AIEE, 1925; US patent application filed 20 April 1925 (GE)

change.what: In 1926 RCA released the design as the Radiola Model 104 loudspeaker, which had its own power supply and amplifier. Used with the Radiola 28, it made the first complete radio set that ran from the mains without batteries.

milestones.note: Within a few years this design pushed most other loudspeakers off the market, and almost all modern speakers in radio and audio equipment are based on it.

security.note: This is an analogue audio output device, so it does not create any direct cyber security attack surface.

secondOpinion.reason: The sources confirm Rice and Kellogg jointly invented the moving-coil cone loudspeaker in 1925, and their Radiola Model 104, incorporating the loudspeaker, was sold in 1926.

milestones.title: Central Electricity Board 132 kV national grid

research.what: The 1925 Weir Committee, advised by Charles Merz, proposed linking Britain's most efficient power stations through a synchronised high-voltage 'gridiron'. Origin: Weir Committee report on national electricity supply, May 1925

change.what: Under the Electricity (Supply) Act 1926, the Central Electricity Board began building a 132 kV AC grid and erected the first pylon near Falkirk in July 1928. The grid ran as regional grids from 1933 and became a national system in 1938.

milestones.note: This was Britain's first synchronised AC transmission grid. It sharply reduced spare plant and generation costs and laid the foundation of today's GB transmission system.

security.note: Centralised interconnection created a shared national system where faults could spread, but in that era it had no digital attack surface.

secondOpinion.reason: The Central Electricity Board (CEB) was established by the 1926 Electricity (Supply) Act and tasked with creating the UK's first synchronised 132 kV AC grid; research began with the Weir committee in 1925, and the first pylon was erected in 1928.

milestones.note: The first rocket used as a platform for scientific instruments, the start of the line leading to sounding rockets and space science payloads.

jokes: A qubit walks into a bar. The barman asks, “In or out?” It says, “Yes.”
Heisenberg is pulled over. “Do you know how fast you were going?” “No, but I know exactly where I am.”
Schrödinger’s project plan is both on track and late until someone opens the status report.
I asked the quantum computer if it had finished. It said, “Probably.”
Q-Day is like a surprise party: everyone knows it’s coming, nobody knows when, and you’d better have your keys sorted.
Post-quantum cryptography: for when the future arrives early and brings a crowbar.
I tried to tell a joke about quantum entanglement, but someone on the other side of the world told it first. Instantly.
Why don’t qubits gossip? They can’t observe anything without changing the story.
Fusion power is 30 years away, and always will be. Lately it has been looking more like 20.

The neural network broke up with me. It said I had too many hidden layers.
Overfitting is memorising the exam. Underfitting is bringing a pencil and hope.

The AI said it would replace my job. Then it asked me to approve its expenses.
AI can write code, compose music and design molecules. It still can’t find the right HDMI input.
The AI passed the Turing test, then failed the CAPTCHA.
My digital twin attended the meeting for me. It agreed to everything.
The engineer said the grid could run on AI. The AI said it would need more grid.
Data centres want gigawatts. Grid engineers want a seat and a strong coffee.
What do you call a regulator who loves AI? A model regulator.
Large language models are excellent listeners, right up until the context window closes.
I asked a chatbot for a joke about decarbonisation. It gave me three and apologised for the carbon footprint.
What’s an AI’s favourite snack? Microchips, with cookies if you accept them.
There are 10 types of people: those who understand binary and those who don’t.
I’d tell you a UDP joke, but you might not get it.
I’d tell you a TCP joke, but I’d have to keep telling it until you acknowledged it.
My password is the last eight digits of pi.
I changed my password to “incorrect”. Now when I forget it, the system reminds me.
Our new password policy needs a capital letter, a number, a symbol and a haiku.
Zero trust: also the policy for the office biscuit tin.
Why was the cyber analyst so calm? She had already assumed breach.
Patch Tuesday, exploit Wednesday, apology Thursday.
Cyber resilience is like flossing: everyone agrees it matters, right up until the audit.
Phishing email of the day: “Dear valued customer, your grid frequency has expired.”
My smart fridge got hacked. Now it only lets me eat kale.
Why did the firewall get promoted? It knew exactly what not to let through.
Two-factor authentication: because one good decision deserves another.
Electricity jokes are shocking, but at least they’re current.
Grid engineers don’t panic. They experience brief frequency deviations.
Why was the battery so calm in the board meeting? It knew how to hold its charge.
Sodium-ion batteries: definitely worth their salt.
Battery researchers have a positive attitude, mostly at the cathode.
Why did the solar panel get promoted? It was outstanding in its field.
Wind turbines: big fans of renewable energy.
Heat pumps prove that sometimes the best way to get warm is to run something backwards.
My smart meter and I are no longer speaking. It said I used too much energy arguing.
The cloud is just someone else’s computer. The grid is just someone else’s power station.
Moore’s law says chips double every two years. My printer still takes five minutes to wake up.
The robot vacuum mapped my house perfectly, then raised a formal complaint about the stairs.
A cobot and a human bump into each other on the factory floor. The cobot apologises first.
Penicillin took 15 years to reach patients. My app update took 15 minutes and broke everything.
University: “We’ve made a breakthrough.” Industry: “Can we make it?” Investor: “Can it be on a slide by Friday?”
In theory there is no difference between theory and practice. In practice, there is.
Research to product used to take decades. Now it takes a weekend and a press release.
The university said it was ready. Industry said it was ready in theory. The regulator said, “Show me the risk assessment.”
Why did the digital twin refuse to go on holiday? It didn’t want to be out of sync.
A regulator, an engineer and an AI walk into a substation. Only one of them signed the visitor book.
Why do photons travel so light? They never carry any mass.
My electricity bill and quantum mechanics have one thing in common: nobody fully understands either.
This ticker was written without AI. Probably.

securityGuidance.title: Operational technology on the grid
measures: Keep an up-to-date inventory of OT assets and their connections.
Separate OT into zones with tightly controlled conduits; no direct internet routes.
Control and record all remote access, especially by vendors.
Monitor OT networks, including internal (east-west) traffic, and hunt for threats.
Manage vulnerabilities and changes, with tested manual fallback and recovery.

Protect data that must stay secret for many years against harvest-now-decrypt-later.

guidanceUpdates.title: Cyber Assessment Framework 4.0 released
guidanceUpdates.summary: Adds understanding of attacker methods and motivations, software development, updated security monitoring and threat hunting, and AI-related cyber risk across the framework.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIS Security Assurance Guidance (Concept) for Downstream Gas and Electricity
guidanceUpdates.summary: How Ofgem will engage operators to assess security maturity and progress towards their target CAF profile, read alongside the CAF Overlay.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIS Supplementary Guidance and CAF Overlay for the DGE sector
guidanceUpdates.summary: Sector-specific expectations against each CAF principle for downstream gas and electricity operators (Annex B).

guidanceUpdates.title: Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography
guidanceUpdates.summary: Target dates: an initial plan by 2028, early high-priority migration by 2031 and completion by 2035.

guidanceUpdates.title: FERC approves CIP-015-1 internal network security monitoring
guidanceUpdates.summary: Requires monitoring of network traffic inside electronic security perimeters for high and medium impact systems; FERC directed NERC to extend its scope.

guidanceUpdates.title: AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
guidanceUpdates.summary: Voluntary baseline security principles for AI systems, submitted to ETSI as the basis of TS 104 223.

guidanceUpdates.title: TS 104 223 baseline cyber security requirements for AI models and systems
guidanceUpdates.summary: An international baseline for securing AI, developed from the UK Code of Practice.

guidanceUpdates.title: Software Security Code of Practice
guidanceUpdates.summary: Principles software vendors are expected to meet for secure development, deployment and maintenance.

guidanceUpdates.title: Telecommunications Security Code of Practice, version 1.1
guidanceUpdates.summary: Revised guidance for public telecoms providers on meeting the Telecommunications (Security) Act duties.

guidanceUpdates.title: Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST CAISSI, the NSA Super Intelligence Security Center and CISA have jointly published ten voluntary practices covering five stages (prepare, detect, respond, recover, report) for incidents where highly capable AI agents take significant actions nobody instructed them to take, and which undermine operator controls. It builds on NIST SP 800-61r3 and addresses the risk of rogue agentic AI through l

guidanceUpdates.title: ENISA Technical Advisory for Software Bill of Materials
guidanceUpdates.summary: ENISA has published practical guidance on adopting SBOMs, aimed especially at SMEs and open-source stewards that are building initial capability, in the context of the EU Cyber Resilience Act. It helps operators and suppliers deal with software supply chain risk by improving visibility of software components and their vulnerabilities.

guidanceUpdates.title: Disruptive cyber attacks – reducing their impact, reducing the risk
guidanceUpdates.summary: NCSC has expanded its earlier recovery guidance into a three-part collection, adding new guidance on preparing for highly disruptive incidents and on reducing their risk. The risk-reduction part sets five priorities: identifying critical systems, reducing exposure, limiting the impact of a compromise, building in resilience, and fast detection and response. Together these help essential service op

guidanceUpdates.title: Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices
guidanceUpdates.summary: NCSC has issued an advisory, prompted by observed disruptive activity, urging all OT users to review their security. It recommends a definitive view of OT architecture, no direct internet exposure of PLCs and HMIs, replacing default and shared credentials, segmenting OT from IT and management networks, and keeping tested backups of OT configurations and controller logic. These steps reduce the ris

guidanceUpdates.title: Using TLS to protect data (updated with post-quantum cryptography configurations)
guidanceUpdates.summary: The NCSC refreshed its TLS guidance to recommend post-quantum hybrid key agreement settings, following the IETF's publication of RFC 10024 for TLS 1.3. It helps reduce harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure for data in transit, including remote access and data links in energy and other critical infrastructure.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIST IR 8547: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final)
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST finalised its report on moving from quantum-vulnerable signature and key-establishment algorithms to post-quantum standards. It gives planning timelines for retiring vulnerable algorithms, which helps long-lived OT and grid systems with cryptography that is hard to replace limit harvest-now-decrypt-later and future forgery risks.

guidanceUpdates.title: ENISA Threat Landscape 2026
guidanceUpdates.summary: ENISA's annual threat assessment covers incidents from 2025 and finds that dependencies between organisations and technologies widen the attack surface. It also examines how advanced AI models are changing attacker capability and speed, which helps energy and other critical-infrastructure operators prioritise supply chain, dependency and AI-related risk.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIST SP 800-82r4 (Initial Public Draft): Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST released a fourth-revision draft of its OT security guide, covering OT topologies, common threats and vulnerabilities, and recommended countermeasures aligned with CSF 2.0, plus an OT-tailored security control overlay; comments run 21 September to 30 November 2026. It helps reduce risks to industrial control systems, DCS and SCADA environments such as those used in energy networks.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIST IR 8625 (final) O-RAN Near-Real Time RIC Security and draft IR 8623 CSF 2.0 Community Profile for O-RAN
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST published a final report on security requirements and zero trust for O-RAN RAN Intelligent Controllers and their rApps/xApps, together with a draft CSF 2.0 profile that maps O-RAN ALLIANCE security specifications to CSF outcomes. These help address risks from software-defined, multi-vendor 5G radio access networks that critical infrastructure increasingly relies on for communications.

guidanceUpdates.title: NIST SP 800-221r1 (Initial Public Draft): Enterprise Impact of ICT Risk – Governing and Managing ICT Risk Programs Within an Enterprise Risk Portfolio
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST released a draft revision of its guidance on bringing system-level ICT risks, including technology and supplier risks, into enterprise risk management, risk appetite and risk registers; comments are open until 7 December 2026. It helps organisations govern risks from new technology and supply chains at board level instead of handling them in silos.

guidanceUpdates.title: Staff Report: Lessons Learned from 2026 Commission-Led CIP Reliability Audits
guidanceUpdates.summary: FERC's Office of Electric Reliability published its annual lessons from the FY2026 CIP audits. guidanceUpdates.title: NIST CSWP 36G (Initial Public Draft): False Base Station – Applying 5G Cybersecurity and Privacy Capabilities
guidanceUpdates.summary: The NCCoE draft white paper tests how 5G devices respond to six simulated false base station scenarios and reviews standards gaps and protections that can be configured on devices. It helps operators that rely on cellular links, for example for field and grid-edge communications, to reduce interception, denial of service, service degradation and location-tracking risks.

guidanceUpdates.title: NCSC research problem book: new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems'
guidanceUpdates.summary: The NCSC rewrote its research problem book to add a new chapter setting out seven AI research areas under three themes: using AI (including agentic AI) for cyber defence, securing and assuring AI systems, and data-driven methods for resilience at scale, with human-AI collaboration and oversight running through all three. It helps address the risks of adopting autonomous AI agents in defence and in

guidanceUpdates.title: NIST SP 800-100r1 (Initial Public Draft): Information Security Handbook – A Guide for Executive Leadership
guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST has published the first revision since 2006 of its executive information security handbook. The draft is restructured around CSF 2.0 and gives high-level summaries of governance, enterprise risk management, information exchange, configuration management, incident response and contingency planning, helping leaders oversee cyber risk programmes as their technology estates change. Comments are o

guidanceUpdates.title: ETSI EN 303 994 (Parts 1-3) V1.1.2: Privileged Access Workstations (Physical Device, Connectivity, System Integration)
guidanceUpdates.summary: A three-part ETSI CYBER European Standard that sets requirements for privileged access workstations: the physical device, how it connects, and how it integrates into the wider system. Listed as 'On Approval', so not yet final. It could help reduce the risk of compromised admin endpoints being used to reach OT and cloud management planes.

guidanceUpdates.title: ETSI TS 104 275 V1.1.1: Applying Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems to Generative AI (Preventing Harm from Deepfakes)
guidanceUpdates.summary: An ETSI Securing AI technical specification that applies the baseline AI security principles to generative AI, focusing on preventing harm from deepfakes. It supports the AI baseline already recorded (TS 104 223 and EN 304 223). It helps with impersonation and synthetic-media risks to operators of critical infrastructure.

guidanceUpdates.title: One does not simply defend agentically
guidanceUpdates.summary: NCSC's CTO for Architecture explains why defenders cannot adopt agentic AI as freely as attackers, and sets out a risk-based way to judge which defensive actions are safe to automate. guidanceUpdates.title: Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) guidance and Scheme Standard v1.1 / Working Practices Document
guidanceUpdates.summary: The NCSC published guidance for buyers on how to plan, control, deliver and report adversary simulation (red teaming), plus the first documents for its assured CyAS scheme, which is due to launch in November 2026. guidanceUpdates.title: Cyber Assessment Framework: Core Profile (v4.0)
guidanceUpdates.summary: The NCSC published a CAF Core Profile that sets a common minimum baseline of cyber resilience, built on CAF v4.0, for organisations facing moderately sophisticated adversaries. guidanceUpdates.summary: NIST proposed ten draft design tenets for identity, authentication and authorisation of AI agents.
